Hello
I’m Councilmember Mark Humbert
I’m excited to announce that I’m running for re-election!
It has been a privilege and a pleasure to serve you and all of my neighbors in District 8 these past four years, and I hope to serve District 8 and Berkeley for another four years. Together, we’ve accomplished a lot:
Enhancing District 8 parks and replacing the Willard Clubhouse with a new, award-winning facility
Passing Measure FF to fund smoother, safer streets
Supporting our first responders with superb chiefs, new tech, and wildfire preparedness
Adopting Middle Housing zoning to enable the creation of smaller, more affordable homes
Supporting the Elmwood Music Festival, Russell Street Halloween, Berkeley Sun Day, and other community events and organizations
And more!
I would be honored to earn your vote again.
Contribution rules:
- I am making this contribution with my own personal credit card and not with a corporate or business credit card or a card issued to another person.
- I am a U.S. citizen or lawfully admitted permanent resident (i.e., green card holder).
- I am at least eighteen years old.
- This contribution is made from my own funds, and funds are not being provided to me by another person or entity for the purpose of making this contribution.
Berkeley residents: please complete and sign the donation matching form and email to mark@humbertforcouncil.com!
About Mark
Mark with his family
I have lived in Berkeley for over 25 years and I feel privileged to have served our City as the District 8 Councilmember for nearly four years now. Berkeley has been a wonderful place to live and raise my family, and I want to continue to give back to our community so that others and their kids can enjoy the same opportunities I did.
As your Councilmember, I have prioritized support for our basic City services and infrastructure, as well as planning for our future. If I have the honor of being reelected for another four years, I intend to maintain this pragmatic and focused approach.
I believe that serving our City and our values demands that we prioritize basic services and infrastructure, especially in lean budget times. I believe in giving Berkeley’s excellent City workers the support (and breathing room) they need to focus on keeping residents safe and healthy, and our roads and civic facilities in the best shape possible.
If elected for another four years, I will stay squarely focused on making sure the things we value most come first, and that City resources are allocated efficiently and consistent with our values.

## Accomplishments in Office
A record of getting things done for District 8 — from safer streets and restored bus service to smart housing policy that protects the neighborhoods we love. Select any item to read the details.
Expand All Collapse All
### Shepherded the now-open and award-winning Willard Clubhouse and Park improvements through final Council approval
Initiated by former Councilmember Lori Droste, Mark brought the Willard Clubhouse and Park improvements over the finish line, navigating tense, last-minute zoning considerations to deliver the final Council vote in support of the project. The old Willard clubhouse was inadequately sized and lacked essential facilities for afterschool care and neighborhood events.
Thanks to Mark and Lori's efforts, it has now been rebuilt as an award-winning, highly sustainable community space. Mark fought to ensure the project was not delayed or watered down, so it could serve as many of our kids and neighbors as possible.
### Spearheaded the “tailored zoning” approach to protect Elmwood’s retail fabric and small businesses and focus new homes on select opportunity sites featuring large parking areas
Mark believes firmly that Berkeley must make good on its promise of being an inclusive community that provides new homes for families, essential workers, and immigrants alike. At the same time, Mark is determined to protect the small and local businesses that give Elmwood its unique character.
That's why Mark spearheaded the “tailored zoning” approach that won formal support from the Berkeley Planning Commission earlier this year. This approach targets zoning changes to the three specific opportunity sites in Elmwood that have the greatest potential for new homes while avoiding impacts to the pedestrian-oriented retail fabric we all treasure. You can read more about his positions on this issue on his Corridors Zoning Update FAQ.
### Championed “quick build” safety improvements for Claremont Avenue to reduce speeding and improve safety for people walking, biking, and driving
Claremont Avenue has long been a dangerous roadway, frequently used by people speeding through between freeways. In response to the most recent tragic loss of life along this roadway, Mark engaged with the community and City staff to develop and kick off a plan for “quick build” safety improvements.
These low-cost strategies represent low-hanging fruit for improving roadway safety by encouraging drivers to slow down and be more aware of their surroundings. These quick-build solutions are currently under construction and serve as a precursor to more extensive long-term improvements anticipated along Claremont Avenue following Alameda County flood control projects beginning later this year or next.
### Successfully persuaded AC Transit to restore bus service on Ashby Avenue
During the pandemic, AC Transit eliminated bus service along Ashby Avenue. Mark was instrumental in persuading AC Transit to bring back an Ashby bus line as the agency considered which services to restore after lockdown. AC Transit was prepared to leave Ashby Avenue without service and instead bring back bus lines elsewhere.
By carefully analyzing AC Transit ridership data, Mark was able to show that the Ashby segment of the prior Line 7 was the more logical and cost-effective choice for restoration. The AC Transit board agreed, and Ashby once again has bus service in the form of Line 27.
### Brokered the Council compromise on middle housing to bring medium-density, naturally affordable homes to more Berkeley neighborhoods
Also first initiated by former Councilmember Droste, Berkeley's Middle Housing efforts aim to promote the creation of new homes in modestly sized projects in Berkeley neighborhoods that previously had exclusionary zoning. This effort culminated in final Planning Commission and Council votes during Mark's time in office.
Faced with competing proposals — one of which would have created fewer homes than we need, and one which would have effectively eliminated certain density limits entirely — Mark helped find the middle path for Middle Housing. He helped broker the deal from the dais that led to a consensus proposal winning broad approval from the Council.
### Eliminated duplicative reporting for police equipment use and led the charge to permanently appoint Berkeley’s Chief of Police
Due to changes in State law, police reporting procedures previously adopted by the City Council were creating duplicative and conflicting requirements. Mark introduced the Council item that streamlined and consolidated these reporting requirements, so the Council and public would still get the information they need — but in a single report that comports with State law.
### Advanced community engagement and design work for safety improvements to Zachary’s Corner and earmarked money for improvements from UC settlement funds
As a member of the UC/City/Student relations committee, Councilmember Humbert fought for UC Berkeley settlement funds to be set aside for the design and construction of safety improvements at Zachary's Corner. Seventeen years ago, this dangerous intersection at Warring and Derby was the site of the tragic loss of five-year-old Zachary Cruz to traffic violence.
Intersection changes to slow down vehicles and improve sight lines have been a long time coming, and Mark insisted that UC settlement funds be prioritized for this project. As a result, community meetings have taken place and a new design has been selected, with construction anticipated to take place soon.
### Funded the Music in the Elmwood Festival, Russell Street Halloween, and Berkeley Sun Day with funds from his office budget
Mark deeply values the community events that bring our neighborhood together. That is why he has reliably provided funding to key community events including Russell Street Halloween, the Music in the Elmwood festival, and the nascent Berkeley Sun Day festival.
Mark has given $1,000 annually from his Council office budget to Russell Street Halloween. And when City bodies declined the Elmwood business association's request for an arts grant, Mark stepped in to provide $7,000 in rescue funds for the Music in the Elmwood festival. Mark is deeply committed to running a lean Council office that leaves room for critical funding for community events.
### Introduced an item to reform Berkeley’s byzantine rules for hot tub installation
After a routine hot tub installation resulted in a lengthy neighbor battle and Council hearing, Mark took action to ensure that such disputes do not routinely bubble up to the City Council. Mark introduced an item to have City planning staff develop revisions to Berkeley's Zoning Ordinance that would standardize and streamline the rules and processes for obtaining permits for new hot tubs. This seemingly small change reduces staff time and costs, and aligns Berkeley with how other cities adjudicate Jacuzzis.
### Fought for fairness and flexibility for ADU and duplex owners
Across multiple efforts to increase regulatory burdens, Mark has fought for basic fairness and flexibility for mom-and-pop landlords who own duplexes or ADUs and live on site with their tenants. Although Mark is broadly supportive of basic tenant protections — especially for those in large and corporate-owned apartment buildings — he recognizes and fights for the idea that the relationship is fundamentally different when you are sharing your home or property with your tenant.
Mark has repeatedly resisted efforts to place onerous requirements on small landlords that could force them to live long-term with problematic tenants. And Mark was the sole vote on the City Council against rules (now overturned by the courts) that would have made it hard for small landlords to determine fair market rents for their units.
### Lobbied state legislators to include Berkeley in pilot programs for speed enforcement cameras
Automated cameras for speed enforcement are a no-brainer for improving safety on Berkeley streets. Unfortunately, the California State legislature has continued to limit their use and failed to expand pilot programs to include Berkeley (or simply all cities across California). When the speed enforcement camera pilot program came before the State legislature, Mark introduced an urgency item to have the City Council urge state legislators to include Berkeley in the pilot. Although the state still has not done so, this continues to be an area of advocacy for Mark.
### Initiated study of 4-way stop improvements for key intersections
Following a series of serious accidents at Berkeley intersections that featured only two-way stops, Mark introduced an item referring to staff a study of improvements at key intersections to slow traffic, increase safety, and pursue newer, more flexible standards for the installation of four-way stop signs.
### Requested full funding for the City 50/50 sidewalk repair program
Under State law, property owners are responsible for repairing sidewalks next to their property; however, the City of Berkeley's 50/50 program splits these costs with property owners to incentivize sidewalk repairs. Unfortunately, this program has been underfunded for years, resulting in long backlogs and poor sidewalk conditions.
Early in his tenure, Mark put forward a budget referral to fully fund this program and speed up repairs. Although the full Council did not ultimately prioritize this expenditure, Mark's goal of fully funding this program has found its way into recent ballot and bond measures.

Elmwood Zoning
I believe that we can protect what makes Elmwood and Berkeley great while also living up to Berkeley values of being an inclusive community that welcomes immigrants and creates the homes our kids will need to build their own families and lives in Berkeley.
### Here’s the short version:
- California law requires Berkeley to zone for at least 9,000 new homes from 2023–2031
- California fair housing laws also require Berkeley to allow for new homes along commercial corridors in high-resource areas, like College Avenue
- The initial proposal would have rezoned all College Avenue shops
- I personally met multiple times with neighbors and leadership of Save Berkeley Shops, and I took their well-founded concerns to heart
- In November 2025 I put forward the “tailored zoning” approach that protects our local shops, and focuses the rezoning on just three high-opportunity sites: the 7-11, the Wells Fargo parking lot, and the Post Office parcel. This rezoning would allow, but not require, the owners of those sites to propose new homes.
- From November 2025 to May 2026 I worked hard to build support on the Planning Commission and among as many councilmembers as I could legally work with
- In May 2026 the Planning Commission voted to recommend my tailored zoning approach, not just for Elmwood, but also North Shattuck and Solano. It will now go before the full City Council so the rest of my colleagues can discuss and, I hope, approve this targeted zoning change that meets our obligations under State law.
### Here’s the long version:
California State law requires Berkeley to make good on the policies in its Housing Element and to affirmatively further fair housing. This means allowing for new homes along commercial corridors in high-resource areas of Berkeley in a way that is equitable with what has been allowed in other areas of town. If we fail to do so, it is possible Berkeley could not only lose funding for affordable and supportive housing, but also lose control of our local zoning through the “builder’s remedy.” If that happened, there would be little limit to the height of what could be proposed and the protections I’ve been fighting for would be in jeopardy.
### My Solution
Happily, I believe we can actually achieve a win-win in Elmwood: Allowing for more homes on targeted, underutilized parcels while preserving the unbroken, pedestrian-oriented retail fabric that makes it unique. That’s why I’m continuing to push hard for my “Tailored Zoning” approach that would focus rezoning on the 7-11, the parking lot behind Wells Fargo, and the Post Office site (if USPS leaves).
We are in a fortunate position: these sites are currently dominated by parking lots and are not significantly contributing to the walkable feel of Elmwood. They also happen to be the three sites that City staff and consultants identified as being the three most feasible for new housing. We can therefore rezone just these three sites, achieve almost the same capacity for new homes that was originally projected for a broader rezone, protect existing retail, and enhance the neighborhood and add more foot traffic for our local shops.
I have championed this Tailored Zoning approach for nearly a year, and I’m very pleased that the Planning Commission has voted decisively in favor of it—though there is one site they changed that I intend to push to fix when it comes to Council. Right now we are waiting for final work on the new zoning to complete and for it to come back before Council, possibly in the late fall. I will work hard to land the Tailored Zoning approach, and I think I’m uniquely positioned to try to get a majority of my Council colleagues on board.
### Correcting Misinformation
I must, unfortunately, also address misinformation that I’ve heard circulating in the neighborhood: Neither the City nor I are seeking to “bulldoze” Elmwood shops; and the Elmwood theater is already a protected landmark that I have fought and will continue to fight to protect. I have been a booster for the Elmwood theater, and when the Elmwood Theater’s big premiere of Oppenheimer was threatened by damage from a car accident, I personally worked with City staff to ensure the theater could reopen on time. Keeping in place the existing landmark that already protects the theater is non-negotiable.
If you would like to read in a lot more detail about the Corridors Zoning Update and housing in general, please check out my CZU FAQ.
ALPRs/Flock
### Here’s the short version:
I support giving BPD the right tools for the job, while also applying rules and oversight to safeguard civil liberties and make sure our data are protected and used appropriately. I will continue to insist that any vendor the City uses be held to a very high and strict standard.
### Here’s the long version:
I want to be candid about this because I feel that Berkeley faces a difficult balancing act and there are multiple things I believe are true:
- Done right, automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are an effective tool to solve and prevent crimes and which help our police department cope with having fewer officers;
- I do not trust Flock because they’ve had multiple instances of carelessness (at best) with other cities’ data;
- Other providers are even less transparent about their practices and are perhaps even more entangled with the Trump administration than Flock; and
- If Berkeley continues using ALPRs, we need an airtight contract with strong data protections, and which we can instantly exit at will and without penalty, regardless of who operates them.
Berkeley and California already have strong prohibitions against sharing ALPR data with federal agencies. This is the legal bare minimum and absolutely non-negotiable. The City is currently engaging in an RFP process to seek alternatives to Flock’s ALPRs.
For me, additional red-line requirements for any future ALPR contract are: strict City control of who can access Berkeley’s data; thorough and regular auditing of who has access and who is searching for what; and, most importantly, contract escape clauses that let the City cancel the contract at any time, for any reason, and with no financial penalty for the City.
Having seen first hand how quick and effective these devices are at catching stolen and crime-associated vehicles coming into Berkeley, I’m convinced that they offer significant public safety benefits. And with strict data controls and contract provisions, I believe Berkeley can make use of ALPRs while respecting civil liberties and protecting the public from abuse of these systems. And if we have any reason whatsoever to suspect abuse, we can pull the plug.
Willard Pool
Like many of you, I deeply miss Willard Pool and wish we could bring it back. South Berkeley has a dearth of public recreation facilities, and the closure of Willard Pool made this scarcity that much worse. Unfortunately, the City Council has few if any tools to resurrect Willard Pool.
Following the defeat of Measure C in 2012, which would have provided bond money to renovate and re-open the pool, the Berkeley Unified School District moved on from the idea of having a pool there. BUSD continues to own the property, and my understanding is that they have not expressed interest in selling it to the City or bringing back a pool at that location.
My sense is that the School District is hoping to someday use all or a portion of the site for a new auditorium at Willard Middle School, which currently only has a less-than-ideal “cafetorium.” Decisions regarding Willard Pool thus rest fundamentally with BUSD, not the City Council. I would welcome a citizen’s initiative provide funding and encourage BUSD to reopen the pool and/or sell the property to the City (this would have the advantage of a lower approval threshold than a Council-initiated measure). But, unfortunately, given BUSD’s current plans and the 2012 defeat of Measure C, the City has not been able to prioritize this versus other easier infrastructure wins.
